evidence_level_values.branded-rct: Branded ingredient with own RCTs (0.9x multiplier) - e.g., KSM-66, Meriva

study_type_values.systematic_review_meta: Meta-analysis or systematic review (6 base pts)
study_type_values.clinical_strain: Probiotic strain clinical evidence (4 base pts)

_metadata._scoring_formula: score = study_type_base_points × evidence_level_multiplier (computed live by scorer, not stored)

_scoring_fields_used.study_type: Determines base points: systematic_review_meta=6, rct_multiple=5, rct_single=4, clinical_strain=4, observational=2, animal_study=2, in_vitro=1
_scoring_fields_used.evidence_level: Determines multiplier: product-human=1.0, branded-rct=0.9, ingredient-human=0.9, strain-clinical=0.65, preclinical=0.3
_scoring_fields_used.score_contribution: Metadata label (tier_1/tier_2/tier_3) reflecting computed score bracket. Not used by scorer.

backed_clinical_studies.effect_direction_rationale: One six-week symptom-endpoint RCT supports this complete formula for adult bloating, gas and abdominal discomfort. Attrition (350 baseline; 219 at week six), sponsor involvement and lack of independent symptom-endpoint replication limit certainty. Two related small mechanistic publications under a shared protocol do not establish additional clinical benefits or independent symptom replication.
key_endpoints: Self-reported bloating, gas and abdominal discomfort
backed_clinical_studies.notes: Evidence is for the whole 24-strain plus pomegranate formulation, not individual strains, skin, heart health or micronutrient synthesis. 350 is the baseline sample of the symptom trial, not a sum across studies. No CFU conversion is known or used. PMID 40944126 and 41750436 share protocol NCT04171466; both report 32 randomized, with 27 and 21 completing respectively. The registration reports 46 actual participants across four arms; unique cohort overlap is unresolved, so counts are not summed. Their microbiome/metabolite and barrier outcomes are not independent symptom replication or demonstrated prevention of antibiotic-associated diarrhea. Trial reports establish the named formula, strain list and total potency, not the commercial label's per-blend or individual-strain quantities. Commercial per-blend allocations remain label-identity constraints only. The signed A032 limited whole-formula decision, accepted by Dr. Pham on 2026-10-26 as attested by Sean, is now encoded for the six-week symptom trial only. Its initial three-day titration is not copied into the separate 91-day mechanistic regimens. Existing exact formula matching remains required; native AFU is not converted to CFU and individual strain effects are not inferred.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: REVIEWED DISEASE-CONTEXT RESEARCH, NON-SCORING. The cited studies concern oral Meriva preparation in osteoarthritis, adjunct psoriasis treatment, and biopsy-confirmed NASH. Their findings do not establish the former stress/anxiety, muscle-recovery, or longevity tags. Osteoarthritis: an open controlled registry, 100 participants, 1 g Meriva/day (200 mg total curcuminoids), eight months. Psoriasis: 63 participants, 2 g Meriva/day as an adjunct to topical corticosteroids, 12 weeks. NASH: 52 participants, 2 g Meriva/day, 72 weeks. These are studied regimens, not newly imposed efficacy thresholds. Keep preparation mass distinct from total curcuminoids and pure curcumin. Existing reference-only handling retains this research while avoiding numerical efficacy outside established applicability. No clinician sign-off or universal lack-of-efficacy conclusion is asserted.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Human evidence exists but is endpoint-, population-, form-, and dose-specific. A seven-RCT meta-analysis reported less post-exercise soreness and short-lived improvement in muscle-damage markers, especially in resistance-training and untrained groups. A 37-RCT meta-analysis reported a modest average body-weight effect, strongest in adults with overweight or obesity and around 2 g/day. A separate systematic review of prolonged use in healthy adults found effects only under specific conditions and raised unresolved long-term TMAO questions. This record is not broad proof of energy, cardiovascular, fat-burning, or athletic-performance efficacy.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: PMID 32154768 pooled seven randomized trials of exercise-induced muscle damage and reported improvements in soreness and some 24-hour biomarkers, while calling for further research. PMID 32359762 pooled 37 randomized trials (2,292 participants) and found modest weight and BMI changes, particularly in adults with overweight or obesity; its dose-response analysis suggested the largest body-weight effect near 2 g/day. PMID 32958033 reviewed 11 prolonged-supplementation studies in healthy adults using 1-4 g/day for 12-24 weeks and concluded that physical-performance effects occur only in specific conditions.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Urolithin A studies distinguish physiological biomarkers from clinical performance. In the four-month ATLAS trial, the prespecified peak-power-output primary endpoint did not differ significantly from placebo. Muscle-strength measures improved, while aerobic-endurance and six-minute-walk improvements at 1,000 mg/day were principally within-group; peak VO2 versus placebo was not significant (p=0.058). Amazentis funded the trial and disclosed employee, board and advisory relationships. The earlier first-in-human study primarily assessed tolerability and mitochondrial biomarkers, not demonstrated durable functional benefit.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: PMID 35584623 randomized 88 middle-aged adults to 500 mg/day, 1,000 mg/day urolithin A or placebo for four months. Peak power output, the primary endpoint, was null between groups; selected strength findings were favorable. The 1,000 mg/day aerobic and walking changes were within-group findings and should not be presented as confirmed between-group efficacy. PMID 32694802 is an earlier first-in-human study of single doses and four-week supplementation, with primary safety/tolerability and secondary biomarker outcomes.

Respiratory (mucolytic) and psychiatric-adjunct evidence is real but condition-specific and more heterogeneous. Signed A094 accepts limited oral exercise-soreness findings only. backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: A 6-month randomized, double-blind, 20-centre trial (PMID 9230243, n=262, NAC 600 mg twice daily, 78% aged 65+) significantly reduced the frequency and severity of influenza-like episodes and shifted cell-mediated immunity from anergy toward normoergy; notably it did not prevent A/H1N1 infection, but only 25% of infected participants on NAC developed symptomatic illness versus 79% on placebo. A 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis of 20 supplementation studies (PMID 39632267) found significantly increased glutathione and reduced TBARS and IL-6, with no significant effect on TNF-alpha, creatine kinase or GSSG. A major review of mucolytic agents in chronic bronchitis/COPD (PMID 31107966) supports benefit in respiratory settings, and a 2018 systematic review/meta-analysis (PMID 29457216) found psychiatric-adjunct evidence that is promising but heterogeneous across diagnoses.

purpose_evidence.rationale: Cardiovascular outcome evidence is mixed across reviews and trials. PMID 31567003 reports studied doses of 376-4000 mg/day; 376 mg is the lowest included exposure, not a demonstrated efficacy cutoff. PMID 32951855 reports reduced risks for several coronary outcomes, but not the overall cardiovascular-event composite. Applicability boundaries and numerical credit are editorial policy in quality_score.json.

EFSA identifies 2-4 g/day EPA+DHA for maintenance of triglyceride levels. PMID 37264945 supports a dose-responsive triglyceride effect, more evident above 2 g/day in hyperlipidemia/overweight populations. PMID 31422671 concerns prescription therapy at 4 g/day and does not establish OTC equivalence or a 2 g treatment guarantee. The updated Cochrane review PMID 32114706 finds high-certainty triglyceride reduction and at most small, outcome-specific coronary benefits; this does not establish universal cardiovascular protection. Full-credit thresholds and interpolation belong to quality_score.json.

PMID 18184094 recommends an average daily intake of at least 200 mg DHA for pregnant and lactating women. This is total intake guidance, not proof of preterm-birth prevention from a 200 mg supplement. Numerical credit is editorial policy in quality_score.json.

The broad review is favorable, but higher-dose benefit varies with baseline DHA status and a large 900 mg trial in a well-nourished population was null. Baseline status is personal fit and cannot change a fixed product-quality score. PMID 34959801 is a mechanistic analysis of the ADORE trial, not an independent replication.
Potentially applicable only to an explicitly resolved depression purpose and an EPA-predominant exposure; the generic omega route does not establish that purpose.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Scope is supplementation outcomes only. PMID 28202713 supports reduced acute respiratory infection risk, clearest in people deficient at baseline. Mood and bone claims were removed because this record does not support them: no mood trial is cited at all, and its musculoskeletal reference (PMID 30293909) found no fracture or fall prevention and no clinically meaningful BMD gain from supplementation. Vitamin D's physiological role in calcium absorption is well established but is not a supplementation outcome and needs its own supporting trial before a bone goal returns here; INGR_CALCIUM and other records still carry Joint & Bone Health. 2024 Endocrine Society guidelines recommend empiric supplementation for specific populations. OWNERSHIP: this file owns INTERVENTION evidence (what a trial showed). Product-facing goal_matches are owned by the bone_health synergy cluster in synergy_cluster.json, which carries the NUTRIENT-FUNCTION relationship (vitamin D aids calcium absorption, NIH ODS) and is unaffected by this record. Do not restore a bone goal here to 'fix' a goal_matches question.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Vitamin B12 is an essential nutrient: NIH ODS documents its requirement for central nervous system development, myelination and function, healthy red blood cell formation and DNA synthesis, with RDAs of 2.4 to 2.8 mcg for adults. Nutritional adequacy is a DRI-authority assessment owned by the dose and nutrition path (rda_optimal_uls.json, nutrition_authority_floor), not by this registry. The one interventional synthesis held here answers a narrower question - cognitive function, depressive symptoms and idiopathic fatigue in people WITHOUT overt B12 deficiency or advanced neurological disorders - and found no effect. That null is not evidence about vitamin B12 generally.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: PMID 33809274 (Nutrients 2021) pooled 16 RCTs and 6,276 participants in 'patients without advanced neurological disorders or overt vitamin B12 deficiency' and found no evidence for an effect of B12 alone or B-complex supplementation on any subdomain of cognitive function and no overall effect on measures of depression; only one study reported idiopathic fatigue, so no fatigue analysis was possible. The NIH ODS Vitamin B12 Health Professional fact sheet documents essentiality, deficiency and recommended intakes. Scope repair 2026-09-18: that null previously carried an ingredient-human effect direction across every B12-containing product; the entry is now a reference-tier anchor and describes only the question its source answered.

Total concentrate mass is not a PAC dose or a verified clinical minimum. Enrollment 8857 belongs only to the November 2023 Cochrane update (which supersedes the April 2023 version); participants from the overlapping 2021 review are not summed. No efficacy is inferred for cranberry seed oil or leaf extracts. applicability.studied_population: Adult nonpregnant women with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections, usually at least two in the previous12months. This is not active-infection treatment or evidence for pregnancy, institutionalized elderly people or incomplete bladder emptying.

backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: The Cochrane review, updated November 2023 (PMID 37947276, fifth update; 50 RCTs, 8857 randomised participants), found in moderate-certainty evidence that cranberry products reduce the risk of symptomatic, culture-verified UTIs (RR 0.70) — in women with recurrent UTIs, in children and in people susceptible after an intervention — with little or no benefit in institutionalised elderly people, pregnant women or people with neuromuscular bladder dysfunction; one trial compared tablets with liquid and two compared PAC doses, so equivalence of preparations and PAC doses stays uncertain. It supersedes the April 2023 version (PMID 37068952). A 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis with trial-sequential analysis (PMID 34473789) also supported cranberry use as an adjunct preventive strategy in susceptible groups.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Human evidence for deglycyrrhizinated licorice is modest but real. The strongest modern trials are on the standardized GutGard extract for functional dyspepsia, H. pylori management, and reflux-related symptoms, while older classic DGL ulcer trials were mixed or negative (PMID 21747893, PMID 23606875, PMID 39929150, PMID 4933135). Retained-source scope and limitations: No advantage over placebo in a 47-person DGL duodenal-ulcer trial (PMID: 4933135) Preparation-specific GutGard dyspepsia symptoms, H. pylori test outcomes and reflux symptoms; not proof of generic ulcer healing (PMID: 21747893; 23606875; 39929150)
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: GutGard placebo-controlled trials showed symptom improvement in functional dyspepsia (PMID 21747893), higher H. pylori clearance than placebo in a 60-day study (PMID 23606875), and faster relief of reflux-related symptoms in a larger 2025 trial (PMID 39929150). By contrast, a classic randomized DGL duodenal-ulcer trial found no advantage over placebo (PMID 4933135), so this entry should stay evidence-cautious.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Human evidence concerns Boswellia serrata extracts for osteoarthritis pain, stiffness and function, not stress, longevity or broad immune benefit. This family-level association does not establish that an unspecified resin extract equals Aflapin or Boswellin Super in standardized composition, dose or onset. Enrollment 545 is the seven-trial 2020 review only; participants from the newer trials are not summed. No generic extract-mass threshold is established here. The former UNII X7B7P649WQ identifies BOSWELLIA SERRATA WHOLE, not an extract, and is not used as an extract identifier. Real-label review (2026-09-05) added the printed extract spellings gum extract, standardized extract, Apres-Flex, Casperome and frankincense phytosome as family-level extract preparations; a bare Boswellia serrata row with only a boswellic-acid form stays unmatched until its source states an extract. The primary outcome uses the locked vocabulary label Joint & Bone Health for osteoarthritis pain, stiffness and function.

backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: A 2020 meta-analysis of 28 randomized trials in type 2 diabetes reported reductions in fasting glucose, HbA1c, insulin, and HOMA-IR with chromium supplementation (PMID 32730903). backed_clinical_studies.notes: Curcumin has one of the largest human supplement trial literatures, with broad meta-analytic support for inflammatory, osteoarthritis, and some metabolic endpoints. However, formulation quality and bioavailability matter materially, and the strongest effects are generally seen with enhanced-delivery products rather than unformulated spice-level curcumin (PMID 39478418, PMID 38945354, PMID 38576215, PMID 40615851).
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: A comprehensive 103-trial meta-analysis found high-credibility evidence for improvements in fasting glucose, CRP, HDL, and body weight, with significant effects across 23 of 42 pooled outcomes (PMID 39478418). Additional umbrella-style work supports anti-inflammatory and endothelial-function biomarker effects (PMID 38945354) and osteoarthritis symptom benefit (PMID 38576215), while newer disease-specific syntheses continue to show reductions in CRP and TNF-alpha in knee osteoarthritis (PMID 40615851).

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Human evidence for berberine is strong in metabolic-health settings, especially for glycemic control and selected lipid outcomes, but much of the literature is short-term, China-centered, and methodologically uneven. The overall signal is still clearly beyond preclinical status (PMID 34956436, PMID 37598753, PMID 36467075, PMID 36941490).
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: Meta-analyses in type 2 diabetes report significant reductions in fasting glucose, HbA1c, insulin resistance, and several lipid markers with berberine (PMID 34956436; PMID 36467075). Separate pooled analyses also show modest improvements in glycemic and insulin-related traits (PMID 37598753) and dyslipidemia endpoints (PMID 36941490). The evidence is favorable overall, but most trials remain short and geographically concentrated.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Both indexed randomized trials explicitly used Sunfiber PHGG supplied by Taiyo Kagaku; the evidence is for that ingredient preparation, not for a complete Nature's Way retail formula. Niv 2016 found selective improvement in bloating/gas, but not overall IBS severity, abdominal pain, stool frequency or quality of life; 121 randomized and 108 entered the reported intention-to-treat analysis, with substantial differential attrition. Yasukawa 2019 studied healthy adults with loose stools, excluding diagnosed IBS; 44 randomized, 42 stool-efficacy and 40 microbiome analyses. Stool form improved but frequency, GI symptom journals and overall physical/mental quality-of-life summaries did not. Microbiome composition is secondary surrogate evidence; neither indexed trial measured clinical immune benefits or increased SCFA production. The 2016 study received commercial support from Pro Natura and Sunwic AB with declared investigator independence. Taiyo funded and supplied the 2019 study, participated in protocol preparation and employed three authors; these are not independently funded replications. These limitations support the reviewed mixed clinical determination under the existing grading policy.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: Niv et al. (2016, PMID 26855665) explicitly tested Sunfiber PHGG in adults with Rome III IBS: 3 g/day for the first week, then 6 g/day for 11 weeks; bloating/gas improved, overall severity and quality of life did not. Yasukawa et al. (2019, PMID 31509971) explicitly tested Sunfiber PHGG at 5 g/day for 12 weeks in healthy adults with loose stools; stool form improved, stool frequency did not, and Bifidobacterium relative abundance was a secondary surrogate. PHGG preparation grams are not dietary-fiber assay grams. Trial amounts are source facts for the existing Dose owner, not additional Evidence deductions.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: The human evidence held on this entry for plain boron is one small randomized placebo-controlled trial: 19 male bodybuilders, 10 given 2.5 mg boron daily and 9 placebo for 7 weeks, with no effect on plasma total or free testosterone, lean body mass or strength. That trial was published twice - PMID 8508192 (Int J Sport Nutr 1993) and PMID 7889885 (Environ Health Perspect 1994) report the same 19 participants and the same measures - so this entry cites two publications of ONE trial, not two trials. Scope repair 2026-09-18: study_type was 'observational' although the source is a randomized controlled trial, and total_enrollment was 30 rather than the 19 the source states. The entry is now held at reference tier - it earns no evidence points - because one small off-axis null trial does not establish ingredient-level efficacy for the bone, joint and multivitamin uses these products carry boron for. Calcium fructoborate was removed from the aliases and excluded in applicability: it is a different compound with its own positive short-term trials, and merging the two materials let a plain-boron null speak for fructoborate products and vice versa. No source on this entry studied bone turnover, joint or inflammatory endpoints, so those key_endpoints were removed.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: PMID 8508192: 'The effect of boron supplementation on lean body mass, plasma testosterone levels, and strength in male bodybuilders' - 19 men, 2.5 mg/day for 7 weeks; plasma boron rose but 'analysis of variance indicated no significant effect of boron supplementation on any of the dependent variables'. PMID 7889885 is the same trial reported in Environmental Health Perspectives ('boron supplementation affects these variables not at all'). Calcium fructoborate trials - CRP, IL-6 and lipid markers over 30 days, and knee discomfort over 14 days - are a separate material and are deliberately not curated here; their identifiers are recorded in scripts/audits/evidence_expansion_2026_09/NULL_SCOPE_AUDIT.md rather than on this entry, and a calcium-fructoborate record would need its own review.

backed_clinical_studies.notes: Human systematic reviews support dietary protein supplementation for modest additional gains in lean mass, muscle size, and strength when paired with sustained resistance training. The reviewed sources include whey, casein, milk, soy, pea, and studied source blends. A generic Protein macro declaration or an unspecified protein powder/blend does not identify one of these sources. Source quality differences remain a Formulation question, and the evidence does not imply further benefit once total daily protein intake is already adequate.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: A 49-study meta-analysis in 1,863 healthy adults found protein supplementation modestly improved resistance-training gains in strength, fat-free mass, and muscle size, with no additional fat-free-mass gain above about 1.62 g/kg/day total protein intake (PMID: 28698222). A whey-specific synthesis in older adults found improved lower-body strength with resistance training, but no significant improvement in handgrip strength, physical performance, or most body-composition outcomes (PMID: 39303495).

key_endpoints: Human synthesis of seven clinical studies found lower total cholesterol, triglycerides and fasting blood sugar and increased HDL-C; LDL-C and HbA1c were not significantly improved. Twenty-seven preclinical studies were analyzed separately (PMID: 34538515).

In 23 children aged 2-13 with nephrotic syndrome, medication plus 1g/day for 2 months produced within-group TC and LDL-C decreases of 116.33 and 94.14 mg/dL; the medication-only control also decreased by 69.87 and 61.13 mg/dL. These are not placebo-adjusted treatment effects (PMID: 12487756)
backed_clinical_studies.notes: Reviewed mixed clinical findings with preparation- and population-specific applicability. PMID 34538515 separates seven human clinical studies from 27 preclinical studies and reports null LDL-C/HbA1c findings alongside positive metabolic biomarkers. PMID 35988871 reports eight direct Spirulina-placebo studies/420 participants, 6–16 weeks, with a small LDL-C reduction and VERY LOW certainty. Its 131-trial/13062-participant total spans eleven nutraceuticals and is not a Spirulina study count. Later lipid review PMID 37263369 supports a lipid biomarker signal, not longevity or cardiovascular-event prevention; overlapping reviews must not be summed as independent trials. The HIV trial reports an antioxidant surrogate without between-group immunological/virological benefit; the pediatric nephrotic-syndrome study reports adjunctive within-group changes. No immune protection, longevity or ordinary-dose muscle-recovery claim is established. The existing conservative rct_single/tier_2 scoring representation is retained; source summaries do not automatically upgrade numerical study-type credit. The HIV and pediatric adjunctive studies are not evidence of general longevity benefit.

key_endpoints: Live B. bifidum MIMBb75 was studied once daily for 4 weeks in 122 IBS patients. Global symptom change was -0.88 versus -0.16 points; overall responders were 57% versus 21%, while adequate relief was 47% versus 11%. Exact-strain findings, not species-wide efficacy (PMID: 21418261).

Heat-inactivated, non-viable HI-MIMBb75 (SYN-HI-001) was studied at 1 billion cells daily for 8 weeks in 443 IBS patients. The primary composite endpoint was reached by 34% versus 19% with placebo. Non-viable cells must not be relabeled CFU or treated as confirmation of the same live preparation (PMID: 32277872).

A B. bifidum BGN4 plus B. longum BORI combination was studied in 63 randomized older adults, with 53 completers analyzed, at 1 billion total CFU/day for 12 weeks. Mental-flexibility, stress and serum BDNF findings belong to the combination, not BGN4 alone; endpoint hierarchy is not established by this bounded extraction (PMID: 32300799).

LIMITATIONS CARRIED DELIBERATELY, verified against the sources on 2026-09-18: the larger synthesis reports substantial heterogeneity (LDL-C I2 = 77%, triglycerides I2 = 62%) and its own PREDICTION INTERVALS CROSS NULL for both (LDL-C -48.29 to 18.13; triglycerides -73.47 to 28.77), meaning a future trial could plausibly show no benefit; only hs-CRP is homogeneous (I2 = 0%). The two syntheses are NOT independent replications - 9 RCTs searched to April 2021 and 5 RCTs searched to December 2022 on the same ingredient and outcomes will substantially overlap - so they are recorded as agreeing, not as confirming one another. The endpoints are physiological and clinical biomarkers, not demonstrated reductions in cardiovascular events. The 500 mg/day floor is supported by the dose range the 9-RCT synthesis itself reports across its included trials, not by one branded preparation; the measured catalog label median is 120 mg/day, so most amla products stay out. SCORING HELD 2026-09-18 (owner decision, direction NOT changed): the record stays positive_weak and keeps its 500-1500 mg/day dose context, but it is held at reference tier so it contributes no points. Reason: the existing primary-mass floor overstates positive_weak evidence here. Measured on DSLD 232044 (Capros amla extract 500 mg as the only scorable active), the chain is primary floor 14.0 x positive_weak 0.85 = 11.9 raw, then rescaled by the generic_botanical_branded archetype reference (11.9 / 18.0 x 20) = 13.2 of 20 - for overlapping syntheses with LDL-C and triglyceride prediction intervals crossing null and biomarker rather than patient-important endpoints. The hold is on this record, not on the floor: no scoring rule was changed.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: PMID 37296402 (2023): 9 RCTs, n=535, amla 500-1500 mg/day for 14-84 days; LDL-C -15.08 mg/dL (95% CI -25.43 to -4.73), VLDL-C -5.43, triglycerides -22.35, hs-CRP -1.70 mg/L. backed_clinical_studies.notes: REVIEWED AND SUPPORTIVE, BUT NON-SCORING. The 2016 Cochrane update reports that Harpagophytum procumbens seems to reduce non-specific low back pain more than placebo, with evidence of moderate quality at best. The exposure it describes is HARPAGOSIDE, not extract mass, and the primary trials state the figures: PMID 10101629 gave Harpagophytum extract WS 1531 at 600 and 1200 mg containing 50 and 100 mg of harpagoside, and PMID 12509627 gave Doloteffin containing 60 mg of harpagoside daily. Measured against the catalog on 2026-09-18: exactly 1 of 25 products states harpagoside on its label (standardised to 1.5% of a 700 mg extract, about 10.5 mg/day) - roughly five times BELOW the lowest studied harpagoside dose. No catalog product currently establishes the studied exposure, so this entry is held at reference tier and contributes no evidence points. No extract-milligram to harpagoside conversion is proposed, and no harpagoside floor is encoded, because the applicability owner compares extract mass and a numeric marker floor there would wrongly pass a 700 mg extract against a 50 mg marker threshold. Correction 2026-09-18: an earlier draft of this entry recorded total_enrollment 2050, which is the whole Cochrane review's participant total across six different herbal medicines, not devil's claw alone; it now records 197, the largest devil's-claw-specific trial.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: PMID 26630428 (Spine 2016, Cochrane update, 14 RCTs and 2,050 participants ACROSS SIX HERBAL MEDICINES): Harpagophytum procumbens, Salix alba, Symphytum officinale, Solidago chilensis and lavender essential oil seem to reduce pain more than placebo, with evidence of moderate quality at best; Capsicum frutescens reduces pain more than placebo. PMID 10101629 (n=197): 600 and 1200 mg of extract WS 1531 containing 50 and 100 mg harpagoside vs placebo over 4 weeks; more pain-free patients on the higher dose (P = 0.027), with the effect concentrated in patients with more severe radiating pain. backed_clinical_studies.notes: REVIEWED AND SUPPORTIVE, BUT NON-SCORING. That senna works as a laxative is not in dispute: PMID 33767108 grades the short- and long-term efficacy of senna as good (grade A) evidence supporting first-line use for chronic constipation. IMPORTANT LINEAGE CORRECTION 2026-09-18: an earlier draft of this entry presented PMID 35943487 as a second independent grade-A review. It is not - it states in its own abstract that it is 'a synopsis of an updated systematic review the authors conducted', so it shares an evidence base with the first and may not be counted as independent confirmation. PMID 29885259 IS independent, but it is modest: 7 RCTs and 444 patients in long-term care, senna superior to or as effective as other laxatives, with the authors noting short trial durations and low quality in some included trials. The applicability problem is potency, not efficacy: the evidence is characterised by SENNOSIDE exposure while catalog labels state senna leaf extract mass, and no source establishes an extract-milligram equivalence. Measured 2026-09-18: 0 of 15 catalog products state sennosides on the label, so nothing establishes the studied exposure and this entry contributes no evidence points. SAFETY IS A SEPARATE OWNER: senna is a stimulant laxative with abdominal pain, cramping, bloating, diarrhoea and nausea reported as common adverse events and dependence and electrolyte concerns on chronic use; those are routed to the safety owner and do not reduce the efficacy direction recorded here.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: PMID 33767108 (Am J Gastroenterol 2021): 'We found good evidence to recommend polyethylene glycol or senna as first-line laxatives'. PMID 35943487 (J Am Assoc Nurse Pract 2022) is a synopsis of the authors' own updated systematic review of 41 randomized trials of at least 4 weeks, reaching the same grade A conclusion - the same evidence base restated, not a replication. PMID 29885259 (2018) is an independent systematic review of 7 RCTs and 444 long-term-care patients in which senna was superior to or as effective as other laxatives, with the authors cautioning that short durations and variable quality leave long-term efficacy and safety inconclusive.
backed_clinical_studies.effect_direction_rationale: positive_strong as a DESCRIPTION of the laxative literature - one grade A systematic review plus an independent long-term-care review agreeing - held at reference tier so it earns nothing, because no catalog label establishes the sennoside exposure the evidence is characterised by. Confidence lowered from high to medium on 2026-09-18 after verifying that PMID 35943487 is the authors' own synopsis rather than a second independent grade-A review. study_type=reference; evidence_level=reference; total_enrollment omitted because no synthesis states a pooled participant total.

Three single-ingredient randomized trials in healthy trained men found no testosterone benefit: 6 g/day for 12 weeks in resistance-trained men (no change in total or free testosterone), 3 g/day in a placebo-controlled crossover in male climbers (no effect on testosterone, calculated free testosterone or luteinizing hormone), and 6 g/day for 14 days in boxers under simulated altitude (no effect on testosterone, cortisol or haematological responses). backed_clinical_studies.notes: Sytrinol combines citrus (Citrus sinensis) polymethoxylated flavones with palm (Elaeis guineensis) tocotrienols. A 2007 trial of 270 mg flavones plus 30 mg tocotrienols daily reported large cholesterol reductions; its report combines two open-label pilots with one double-blind arm. An independent 2015 double-blind trial of the same two ingredient classes at lower doses found no effect beyond placebo. Evidence is mixed; only the 300 mg/day exposure was positive.
backed_clinical_studies.notable_studies: Roza et al. (2007, PMID 17985810): 120 hypercholesterolemic adults randomized to 300 mg/day (270 mg citrus flavonoids + 30 mg tocotrienols) or placebo for 12 weeks, plus two 4-week open-label groups of 10; total cholesterol fell 20-30% and LDL 19-27%. Schuchardt et al. (2015, PMID 25828621): 240 adults with elevated LDL-C and hsCRP randomized to 12 mg tocotrienols + 103 mg flavones, 27 mg + 32 mg, or placebo for 12 weeks; no difference in LDL-C or hsCRP versus placebo.
